keyVerseText: Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war. the company: or, the beasts of the reeds scatter: or, he scattereth
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb רָפַס (râphaç) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the physical action of stamping or treading down. This literal sense of pressing or trampling evokes the image of humbling oneself by prostration or submission. Beyond the English glosses like 'humble' or 'submit,' the root sense emphasizes a tangible lowering or pressing down, which enriches the spiritual concept of humility as an active, embodied posture rather than a mere attitude.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only twice in Scripture, consistently carrying the core idea of submission or humbling oneself. Its translations range from 'till every one submit' to simply 'humble,' indicating a focus on yielding or lowering oneself before another. The limited occurrences suggest a specialized usage that highlights deliberate self-abasement or surrender, whether in a physical or figurative sense.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding רָפַס as a verb of deliberate self-humbling deepens our grasp of biblical humility as more than an internal disposition; it involves a conscious, active submission to God's authority. This aligns with the Christian call to deny self and take up the cross, reflecting Christ's own humility. Recognizing the verb's root meaning reminds believers that true faith involves a tangible posture of surrender, not just mental assent. It also underscores the necessity of humbling oneself to receive God's grace and guidance.
keyVerseReflection: In Psalm 68:30, the phrase 'till every one submit himself with pieces of silver' uses רָפַס to convey the idea of stamping down or humbling until full submission is achieved. This highlights the thoroughness of God's call to humility among His people, even in the midst of conflict ('scatter thou the people that delight in war'). The verb enriches the verse by portraying submission as a deliberate and forceful act, not passive acquiescence.
